statement: In people on a stable once-daily methadone dose in an Australian public programme (18 people studied over one 24-hour dosing interval, published 1999), the 9 who reported regular withdrawal before their next dose, compared with the 9 who did not, had a similar methadone level just before the dose (257 against 249 ng/mL) and similar overall exposure, but their level fell faster after the daily peak: fastest fall 74.5 against 47.6 ng/mL per hour, a difference that was not significant in all 18 (P = .09); the paper reports it as significant after 2 people whose urine showed other opioids were left out, but the editors' recalculation gives a two-sided P of about .054. On average, withdrawal symptoms were fewest in the hours after the dose and rose as methadone levels fell, and people whose levels fell fastest reported more withdrawal symptoms (r = 0.60). The groups were formed by self-report, and the study tested no change in treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small study of people on methadone, those who felt withdrawal before their next dose had about the same methadone level as others just before the dose, but their level dropped faster after its daily high point. Only 18 people were tested for one day, and the difference was clear only after two people were left out.
population: People on stable once-daily methadone maintenance in the South Australian public programme (in treatment 6 months to 10 years): 9 who reported regular withdrawal between doses and 9 who did not
exposure: Pattern of plasma methadone over the dosing interval, in particular the fastest hourly fall after the peak
comparator: People on methadone who did not report withdrawal between doses
outcome: Self-reported withdrawal between doses (group) and number of withdrawal symptoms over the interval
magnitude: Level before the dose 257 against 249 ng/mL (P > .05); AUC 8.2 ± 3.9 against 7.4 ± 5.0 mg·h/L (P > .05); fastest fall 74.5 ± 40.4 against 47.6 ± 21.3 ng/mL/h, t = 1.77, P = .09; without 2 people with other opioids in urine 74.5 against 42.1, t = 2.10, stated P < .05 (two-sided P about .054 on 14 degrees of freedom, editors' calculation); correlation of the fastest fall with withdrawal symptoms r = 0.60 (n = 18), r = 0.67 (n = 16).

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity in holders and nonholders, 1st paragraph (p. 690); Figure 2 (p. 689)
evidence.extracted: Withdrawal significantly higher in nonholders and strongly inversely related to plasma methadone in both groups; plasma methadone before the dose 249 ng/mL in holders and 257 ng/mL in nonholders (P > .05); peak-to-trough ratio 1.9 and 1.7 (P > .05); AUC 7.4 and 8.2 mg·h/L (P > .05).

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacokinetics and withdrawal severity in holders and nonholders, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3 and legend
evidence.extracted: Fastest hourly fall in plasma methadone 47.6 ± 21.3 ng/mL/h in holders against 74.5 ± 40.4 in nonholders, t = 1.77, P = .09; without the two people with other opioids in urine 42.1 ± 20.8 against 74.5 ± 40.4, t = 2.10, stated P < .05; correlation of the fastest fall with the mean number of withdrawal symptoms from peak to trough r = 0.60 in all 18 (P < .01) and r = 0.67 without the two. By editors' calculation the two-sided P for t = 2.10 on 14 degrees of freedom is .054.

evidence.locator: Results › Pharmacodynamic responses › Subjective responses (p. 689); Figure 1 (p. 688)
evidence.extracted: Withdrawal symptoms were significantly more frequent in the patients than in the drug-free controls at all times and least severe in the hours after the dose; the MBG positive-effect score peaked a few hours after the dose and returned to baseline later in the interval.

evidence.locator: Results › Plasma concentration-effect relationships, 1st paragraph (p. 690); Table I (p. 691)
evidence.extracted: Slope factor N for withdrawal 5.4 ± 0.9 (model fitted in 9 of 18) and for MBG 5.1 ± 1.05, against 1.2 ± 0.1 for pupil diameter: very steep concentration-effect relationships for withdrawal and positive effects; no significant difference between holders and nonholders (P > .05).

evidence.locator: Methods › Patients and control subjects, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Nine self-reported holders and nine self-reported nonholders volunteered from the South Australian Public Methadone Maintenance Program (in treatment 6 months to 10 years, no dose change for at least 2 months); 11 men and 7 women aged 21 to 45; urine positive for cannabinoids in 10 and for other opioids in 2; 10 drug-free controls.
In the authors' earlier survey in the same programme, 34% of 114 non-selected patients regularly had withdrawal between doses and 66% did not; plasma methadone was not measured there.

The authors caution that methadone is a mixture of two mirror-image forms whose different handling can create apparent distribution effects, so a distribution (disposition) mechanism for the holder-nonholder difference should be invoked with extreme caution; analysis of the active form was under way.

risk_of_bias.note: Groups formed by self-report; the key difference significant only after a post hoc exclusion; the abstract reports only the subset; several P values do not match their test statistics (card sc_dyer_1999, ROBINS-E high).

indirectness.note: Worded for people on stable methadone in this programme.

imprecision.note: 9 people per group; the group difference has a P between .05 and .10.

grade.reasoning: Observational, so it starts low; risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low. The within-person link between falling levels and withdrawal (r = 0.60 in all 18) is firmer than the holder-nonholder difference in the rate of fall. The authors' recommendations about dose scheduling were not tested and are not part of this claim (no regimens on the site). Status single study: earlier studies cited by the authors point the same way but were not read.
